lessons.title: Two Pointers Pattern Overview
lessons.concept: The two pointers technique uses two indices (pointers) to traverse a data structure, often an array or string, to reduce unnecessary work. Depending on the problem, pointers may move toward each other, in the same direction, or at different speeds.
lessons.formula: Common forms: (1) opposite ends: left=0,right=n-1 move inward; (2) slow/fast or read/write: both move forward. Often reduces O(n^2) brute force to O(n) on sorted or linear scans.
lessons.worked_example: Check if sorted array [1,2,3,4,6] has two numbers summing to 7: left=1,right=6 sum=7 -> found. If sum too small move left++, if too large move right--.
mistakes: Applying opposite-end two pointers on an unsorted array when sorting/order assumption is required
Moving the wrong pointer for the condition
Off-by-one errors in loop bounds (e.g., using left <= right vs left < right)

lessons.title: Opposite-End Pointers
lessons.concept: Opposite-end pointers start at both ends of a sequence and move inward based on comparisons. This is common for pair problems in sorted arrays (like pair sum) and palindrome checks.
lessons.formula: Initialize left=0, right=n-1. While left < right: evaluate condition; if need larger value left++; if need smaller value right--; if match record/return.
lessons.worked_example: Palindrome check for 'racecar': compare r==r, a==a, c==c, e==e moving inward -> palindrome. For 'hello', h!=o at ends -> not a palindrome.
mistakes: Forgetting input must be sorted for pair-sum logic to be correct
Not handling duplicate values when the problem requires unique pairs
Infinite loops when pointers are not updated in all branches
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Same-Direction (Fast/Slow or Read/Write) Pointers
lessons.concept: Same-direction pointers move forward through the array, often at different roles or speeds. A common use is in-place filtering/removal (read pointer scans, write pointer tracks position for kept elements) or cycle detection in linked lists (fast/slow).
lessons.formula: Read/write: write=0; for read in range(n): if keep(arr[read]): arr[write]=arr[read]; write+=1. Fast/slow (linked list): slow=slow.next, fast=fast.next.next.
lessons.worked_example: Remove value 2 in-place from [1,2,2,3]: read scans all, write keeps [1,3]; result prefix length 2.
mistakes: Advancing write pointer even when element should be skipped
Confusing array read/write pointer use with linked-list fast/slow use
Not returning/using the new logical length after in-place compaction

practice.explanation: Two pointers often optimize problems by scanning with two indices strategically, reducing redundant work (e.g., from O(n^2) to O(n)) in suitable cases.

practice.question: In a sorted array, to find a pair with a larger sum using opposite-end pointers, which move is correct when current sum is too small?
practice.explanation: In an ascending sorted array, increasing the left pointer can increase the sum, while decreasing the right pointer would make it smaller.

practice.question: For opposite-end pair search, why is a sorted array often required?

options.A: Because pointers cannot index unsorted arrays
options.B: Because pointer movement decisions rely on order to know how sum/value changes
options.D: Because unsorted arrays cannot have pairs

practice.explanation: The correctness of moving left/right depends on monotonic ordering: moving left up increases values, moving right down decreases values.

practice.question: In an in-place array compaction using read/write pointers, the write pointer advances when:

options.B: Only when an element should be kept
options.C: Only when an element should be removed
options.D: At the end of the array only

practice.explanation: The write index marks the next position for a retained element, so it increments only after writing/keeping a valid element.

practice.question: Fast and slow pointers in a linked list are commonly used to:

options.B: Detect cycles or find middle elements

practice.explanation: Different pointer speeds help detect cycles (they meet) and locate the middle (fast reaches end when slow reaches middle).

questions.question: What is a common time complexity benefit of using two pointers instead of checking all pairs in a sorted array pair-sum problem?
questions.explanation: A brute-force pair check is O(n^2), while the opposite-end two-pointer scan over a sorted array runs in O(n).

questions.question: When using read/write pointers to remove elements in-place, what does the write index typically represent at the end?

options.C: The index of the maximum element always
options.D: The number of removed elements only

questions.explanation: Since write increments after placing each kept element, its final value equals the number of retained elements (new logical length).

questions.question: Which statement about fast/slow pointers in linked lists is correct?

options.A: Fast pointer moves one step, slow moves two steps
options.B: If there is a cycle, fast and slow pointers can eventually meet

questions.explanation: Typically slow moves 1 step and fast moves 2; in a cycle, fast gains on slow and they will meet inside the cycle.
